title: Partitioning and sharding: splitting a table, and splitting a database
dek: Both split data into smaller pieces, and the two words are often used for the same thing. The useful difference is where the pieces live: partitioning divides a big table inside one database, so queries and maintenance touch less of it; sharding puts the pieces on different machines, so the work itself is shared. Partitioning is often the step before sharding, and sometimes it is enough.

items: Partitioning splits a large table into pieces inside one database: by rows (one partition per month) or by columns (rarely used, large columns kept apart). No new machines; queries and maintenance touch only the pieces they need.
Sharding is splitting rows across many machines. Each shard is a complete database with its own CPU, memory, disk and connections, so capacity grows with the number of shards.
Sharding brings new jobs: choosing a key, routing queries, avoiding hot shards and rebalancing as data grows.

body.x: Take Zotato's orders table after a few years: 50 crore rows and 2 TB. A query for last month's orders has to search the whole table unless an index narrows it, and the indexes themselves are enormous. Routine maintenance, such as vacuuming, refreshing statistics or rebuilding an index, works on the whole table at once and can slow everything else down.

Partitioning splits that table into smaller tables the database manages separately, while your queries still use one table name. Nothing leaves the machine; the data is just organised into pieces. Now a query for last month reads one month's partition instead of the whole table, and old partitions can be archived or dropped in one cheap step.

body.cap: The orders table split by month inside one database. A query for October reads one partition; dropping 2022 is one quick operation instead of deleting crores of rows.

items: Horizontal partitioning splits rows: one partition per month or year of orders. Every partition has the same columns and fewer rows. This is what 'partitioning' usually means (Postgres's PARTITION BY RANGE, LIST or HASH).

Vertical partitioning splits columns: the small, often-read columns of an order (id, status, total) in one table, and large or rarely read ones (the full delivery instructions, the receipt PDF's text) in another. Same rows, fewer columns per piece, so the hot table fits better in memory.
Partitioning doesn't add capacity: one machine still does all the work. It makes that machine's work more efficient, which can postpone sharding for a long time.

body.cap: Vertical partitioning: the columns read on every screen stay together in a small, hot table; the large, rarely read columns move to a second table with the same ids.

body.x: Sharding is horizontal partitioning across machines. Each shard holds a subset of the rows, and all the shards together hold the whole dataset. Unlike partitions, shards don't share a machine: each is an independent database with its own CPU, memory, storage and connection pool.

body.cap: Orders split by id across three databases. No machine holds all the data or takes all the traffic, so storage and throughput grow by adding shards.

items: Because no single machine holds all the data or serves all the requests, both storage and read and write throughput grow as you add shards.
The application, a routing layer or the database itself must now send each query to the shard that holds the data.

And you take on new problems: choosing a shard key, avoiding hot shards, queries and transactions that span shards, and moving data when shards are added. The articles 'Shard keys and how to spread them' and 'What sharding breaks' cover them.

items: If a table is just big, partition it by time first, and archive old partitions.
Shard only when one machine can't hold or serve the data.
Use the words carefully, but don't argue about them: say whether the data is on one machine or many.
